name: June Halvorsen
equipment: School lanyard (Eastgate Magnet High School, Science Department) and a whistle she has never once blown
Field-trip clipboard with a permission-slip list of twelve names, three of them still with her
Tote bag: a chemistry teacher's emergency kit — nitrile gloves, safety glasses, pH strips, a digital thermometer, a 9-volt battery, a coil of copper wire, a roll of electrical tape and a lighter
Small digital voice recorder (she uses it to tape her own lectures), with spare AAA batteries (4)
A paperback of 'The Periodic Table' by Primo Levi, much underlined
Phone (48% battery) and a cheap pair of wired earbuds
Fire extinguisher, liberated from the Union Terminal concourse wall
features: Human (Specialist) (+2 Intelligence, +1 Wisdom, one extra skill proficiency: Perception)
Analyze (bonus action: study a creature, device or situation; the next attack roll or check an ally makes against it before her next turn has advantage; 3 uses per short rest)

Polymath (proficiency in Science plus Mechanics and Computers; she adds half her proficiency bonus, rounded down, to any Intelligence check she is not proficient in). Her Academic background's Science overlaps Polymath, so it was replaced with Medicine
Faculty Access (Academic feature: university and school staff, librarians and museum curators will let her into labs, stacks and staff areas and take her questions seriously)
The extinguisher can also be discharged: an action, 15-ft cone, every creature in it makes a DC 11 CON save or is blinded until the end of its next turn (5 uses). It is loud and very novel

personality.traits: I narrate what I see in complete sentences, out loud, because it is the only way I can think when I am frightened. I correct people's units. I am almost entirely unafraid of anything I can measure.
personality.ideals: Observe, hypothesise, test. The universe is not cruel and it is not kind, it is consistent — and if these things are consistent, they can be understood, and if they can be understood we can get out from under them.
personality.bonds: Three children: Marisol Peña, DeShawn Archer and Pilar Wu, seventeen, sixteen and sixteen, the three of my twelve AP Chemistry students who were still with me on the concourse when it happened. I signed for them. I signed for all twelve.
personality.flaws: I am a forty-six-year-old woman who has not run since 2003, and my body is going to fail me long before my curiosity does. And I will stand in the open taking notes on a thing that is about to lift me off the street, because I want to know.

appearance: A tall, stooped, Minnesota-pale woman of forty-six with grey-blonde hair in a clip that has given up, tortoiseshell glasses, a long cardigan, a sensible raincoat and a lanyard. Her hands are stained at the fingertips with something that does not wash out. She stands like she is about to write on a board, and when she is thinking hard she taps two fingers against her collarbone in a rhythm only she can hear.
backstory: June Halvorsen has taught AP Chemistry at Eastgate Magnet for nineteen years, and she is the kind of teacher students come back to see at Christmas. She came to Merriwick for a doctorate in physical chemistry, left the programme a year short when her father was dying, and never went back, and she tells herself she does not mind. On the Thursday she is bringing twelve students back from the Natural History Museum's new exhibit on deep-sea acoustics — they were bored, she was enthralled — and she has them herded on the Union Terminal concourse for the 4:20 Blue Line when the light changes. In the stampede that follows she loses nine of them. Three stay with her because she grabs them: Marisol, DeShawn and Pilar. She does not know yet that the other nine are, in fact, fine — they did what teenagers do and kept walking to the subway — and she will spend most of the first night finding that out. She is also the first person on the island to notice, about forty minutes after the Arrival, that the things in the street are ignoring everybody who is walking at a normal pace in a straight line, and she writes it down.
